nameStory: This little plant gets its "mouse-ear" name from its small, oval leaves that are covered in soft hairs, making them feel fuzzy just like a mouse's ear. The "sticky" part comes from the plant's glandular hairs that make it feel slightly tacky or clammy when you touch it. "Chickweed" refers to the fact that chickens and other birds love to eat plants in this family.
description: Sticky mouse-ear chickweed is a small, low-growing annual plant that forms spreading mats close to the ground. It rarely grows taller than 6 inches and has a somewhat sprawling habit with multiple branching stems. The entire plant is covered in soft, grayish hairs that give it a fuzzy appearance and sticky feel. Its tiny white flowers bloom in dense clusters at the stem tips, creating small patches of white against the gray-green foliage.

idTips.label: Sticky Feel
idTips.description: The whole plant feels noticeably sticky or clammy when you touch it due to tiny glandular hairs - this tacky sensation is your best identifying feature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves are densely covered in soft, whitish hairs that make them feel like velvet and give them a grayish-green color

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with 5 deeply notched petals that look almost split in half, clustered tightly together at stem tips

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats with multiple branching stems that rarely exceed 6 inches tall, often growing in dense patches

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems are hairy and feel slightly sticky, often reddish at the base and branching frequently near the top

habitat: Look for sticky mouse-ear chickweed in disturbed soils like garden beds, roadsides, vacant lots, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in sandy or gravelly soils and is often found in areas with poor drainage or compacted earth. This European native has adapted well to urban and suburban environments where it grows as a common weed.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming time with clusters of tiny white flowers most visible from February through May. The sticky, fuzzy texture is most pronounced during active growth.
seasonality.summer: Plants may continue flowering into early summer but often become less noticeable as they complete their annual life cycle and dry out.
seasonality.fall: Seeds disperse and new plants may germinate in favorable conditions, appearing as small rosettes of fuzzy leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.winter: In milder winters, some plants may persist as small leafy patches, but most die back completely until spring germination.

funFact: This plant is like nature's sticky note - its glandular hairs are so effective at trapping small insects that some people mistake it for a carnivorous plant, though it actually just uses the stickiness to prevent ants from stealing nectar meant for flying pollinators!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common mouse-ear chickweed, but the sticky feel is your instant giveaway - common mouse-ear feels soft and hairy but not sticky or clammy. Remember: "Sticky stays, common doesn't cling."
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with other plants called "chickweed" - there are many unrelated species that share this common name because birds enjoy eating them. The mouse-ear chickweeds belong to the pink family, despite their white flowers, because family names often come from the most showy members of the group.
compareHints: Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, sticky mouse-ear is the only one with that distinctive clammy, tacky feel from its glandular hairs. Common mouse-ear chickweed feels soft but dry, while snow-in-summer has much showier, larger white flowers and silvery-white foliage. The sticky texture combined with the tightly clustered small flowers makes this species unmistakable once you know what to feel for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its mouse-ear chickweed relatives, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and persistent in New England.
Snow-in-summer stands out dramatically from its mouse-ear chickweed relatives due to its distinctive 'tomentose' or felty white hairs covering the entire plant, giving it a silvery appearance.
Field chickweed stands out from its mouse-ear relatives by forming the densest, most mat-like growth habit and having the most deeply notched flower petals.
American field chickweed differs from other Cerastium species by having the most deeply divided petals - they're split nearly to the base.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and has the most consistently fuzzy texture throughout the plant.
Little mouse-ear is smaller and more delicate than common mouse-ear chickweed, which is perennial and has longer petals.
Unlike the very common mouse-ear chickweed which has fuzzy, spoon-shaped leaves and upright flowers, nodding chickweed has narrower leaves and distinctively drooping flowers.
Among its mouse-ear relatives, dwarf mouse-ear stands out for being the tiniest and having petals that don't extend beyond the sepals.
